usedCourseFacts.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
usedCourseFacts.name: Personal & Professional Development
usedCourseFacts.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
usedCourseFacts.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
usedCourseFacts.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

usedCourseFacts.description2: Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law, excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners and a moot court session.
usedCourseFacts.name: Law, Society & Justice
usedCourseFacts.profile: Introduces law through legal, social and normative perspectives. Students compare major legal traditions and survey public and private law, including constitutional, criminal, international, human-rights, property, contract and tort law. The second part examines justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, legal interpretation, demand letters and mock trials apply legal reasoning; a family-law topic supports the design of a small socio-legal research proposal.
usedCourseFacts.topics: Legal positivism and empirical and normative perspectives; Common-law and civil-law traditions; Constitutional and administrative law; Criminal law; International law and human rights; Property, contract and tort law; Justice; Law and social control; Law and social change; Race and gender in law; Family law
usedCourseFacts.methods: Legal interpretation; Case-law research and IRAC case briefing; Demand-letter drafting; Mock-trial legal argumentation; Socio-legal research design; Literature review

usedCourseFacts.description2: Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation. The class fosters creativity and collaboration to drive business and social innovation.
usedCourseFacts.name: Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations
usedCourseFacts.profile: Introduces entrepreneurship and core business functions through the development of a startup concept. Students use design thinking to discover customer needs, define a problem, generate and prototype solutions, and construct value propositions and business models. Marketing, finance, operations, human resources and funding inform a coherent business plan and investor pitch. Entrepreneurial cases and a startup simulation examine decision-making, early growth and business lifecycles, with attention to societal impact and sustainability.
usedCourseFacts.topics: Entrepreneurial mindset and pathways; Business environments, ownership and competition; Customer needs; Value propositions; Business models; Marketing and sales; Finance and accounting; Venture funding; Operations and human resources; Competitive positioning; Startup growth and business lifecycles; Sustainability and societal impact
usedCourseFacts.methods: Design thinking; Customer-needs discovery; Ideation and prototyping; Value Proposition Canvas; Business Model Canvas; Business planning; SWOT and risk assessment; Startup simulation

usedCourseFacts.description2: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
usedCourseFacts.name: Introduction to Economics
usedCourseFacts.profile: Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.
usedCourseFacts.topics: Supply and demand; Game theory; Rational consumer choice; Individual and market demand; Production and costs; Perfect competition; Aggregate output; Unemployment and inflation; Goods and financial markets; IS-LM model
usedCourseFacts.methods: Algebraic and graphical economic analysis; Supply-and-demand analysis; Game-theoretic analysis; IS-LM modelling

usedCourseFacts.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
usedCourseFacts.name: Research Methods & Statistics
usedCourseFacts.profile: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
usedCourseFacts.topics: Scientific inquiry and hypotheses; Operationalization and measurement; Reliability and validity; Survey construction and sampling; Randomized and quasi-experimental designs; Nonexperimental and qualitative research; Descriptive statistics; Sampling distributions and estimation; Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals; Association and regression; Research ethics and anonymous data collection
usedCourseFacts.methods: Survey design; Probability and nonprobability sampling; Experimental and nonexperimental research design; R and R Commander data analysis; Descriptive statistics and visualization; Scale-reliability analysis; One- and two-sample mean tests; ANOVA; Chi-square tests; Correlation and regression; Empirical data collection and analysis

usedCourseFacts.description2: Introduces rules, institutions and politics of public international law. Covers treaties, the UN, armed conflict, war crimes, refugee protection and climate change. Students analyse cases, debate issues and produce a podcast connecting law to global challenges.
usedCourseFacts.name: Introduction to Public International Law
usedCourseFacts.profile: Introduces public international law through its sources, theories, institutions and relationship to domestic legal systems. Legal principles are applied to responsibility, force, armed conflict, international crime, human rights, economic relations and environmental protection. The later course examines self-determination, Third World approaches, soft law, compliance and treaty politics. Case exercises develop legal reasoning, while a research podcast critically investigates a political dimension of international law.
usedCourseFacts.topics: Sources and theories of international law; Treaty law; International legal subjects; Jurisdiction and immunities; Domestic courts and international law; State responsibility; Use of force; UN reform; Armed conflict and international criminal law; International human rights and economic law; Environmental law; Self-determination; Third World Approaches to International Law; Soft law, compliance and effectiveness; Global environmental treaties
usedCourseFacts.methods: Identification and interpretation of international legal instruments; Judgment and case-law analysis; Application of legal principles to factual scenarios; Legal, empirical and normative critique; Research podcast development

usedCourseFacts.description2: Explores constitutional law and state organisation, using a comparative approach. Covers constitutionalism, separation of powers, judicial review, federalism and fundamental rights, and discusses constitution‑making, religious constitutions and constitutional backsliding.
usedCourseFacts.name: Comparative Constitutional Law
usedCourseFacts.profile: Compares constitutional structures, institutions and rights across legal systems and introduces administrative law. Students examine constitutional features, federalism, legislatures, executive relationships, courts, judicial review and human rights. The administrative component addresses public participation, remedies and procedural fairness. A staged booklet compares two constitutions, supported by legal interpretation, case-law analysis and application of principles to hypothetical facts.
usedCourseFacts.topics: Constitutional origins and fundamental features; Federalism and decentralization; Parliaments and lawmaking; Governments and heads of state; Court systems and judicial review; Constitutional rights; EU constitutional order; Administrative-law functions; Public participation; Administrative remedies; Procedural fairness, discretion and legitimate expectations
usedCourseFacts.methods: Comparative constitutional analysis; Constitutional and legislative interpretation; Case-law analysis; Application of legal principles to hypothetical facts; Structured comparative legal writing

usedCourseFacts.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
usedCourseFacts.name: Ethics
usedCourseFacts.profile: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
usedCourseFacts.topics: Divine command and human nature; Moral relativism and universalism; Utilitarianism and consequentialism; Kantian ethics; Virtue ethics; Social contract and intuitionism; Feminist and care ethics; Nietzschean genealogy and nihilism; Murdoch's sovereignty of good; Moral value and perspective; Death, absurdity and meaning; Ethical theory and practical judgment
usedCourseFacts.methods: Close philosophical text analysis; Reconstruction and critical evaluation of moral arguments; Comparison of ethical theories; Conceptual analysis; Independent philosophical argument development

usedCourseFacts.description2: Examines principles of property law, tort law, contract law and other fields within private law. Uses comparisons of legal systems in four countries to explore rights and obligations arising from daily interactions.
usedCourseFacts.name: Principles of Private Law
usedCourseFacts.profile: Examines property, tort and contract law through comparison of legal systems, primarily Germany, France, England, China and the United States. Students analyze rights and obligations, ownership, nuisance, negligence, contract formation and fairness, remedies and related policy pressures. Legal issue briefs apply the IRAC method. An issue-based comparative contract-law paper and simulated mediation develop comparative analysis, legal argument and negotiation.
usedCourseFacts.topics: Possession and ownership; Nuisance and property restrictions; Easements, covenants and servitudes; Necessity; Tort structure, intent and negligence; Duties to act; Offer and acceptance; Pre-contractual liability and mistake; Contract fairness and excuse; Specific performance and damages; Unjust enrichment; Mediation and dispute resolution; Private law and public policy
usedCourseFacts.methods: Functional comparative legal analysis; IRAC legal briefing; Case-law analysis; Application of doctrine to hypothetical facts; Comparative contract-law research; Mediation-position drafting; Simulated mediation and negotiation

usedCourseFacts.description2: This course describes the most widely accepted accounting theory and practice with an emphasis on using and analyzing the information in financial statements. Students learn how to comprehend a typical corporate annual report and to use accounting as a tool in understanding how economic events affect business.
usedCourseFacts.name: Accounting & Corporate Finance
usedCourseFacts.profile: Introduces financial accounting, management accounting and investment appraisal, including accounting's social role and accountability implications. Students record transactions, prepare and interpret financial statements, and analyze performance and financing. The course then examines costing, pricing, budgeting, organizational control and sustainable management accounting. Investment decisions are evaluated using accounting and discounted-cash-flow measures. A case study analyzes the misuse of an accounting principle and its financial-statement effects.
usedCourseFacts.discipline: Financial accounting; Management accounting; Corporate finance
usedCourseFacts.topics: Accounting and accountability; Financial reporting frameworks; Accrual accounting; Assets, liabilities and equity; Financial statements and cash flows; Accounting judgements and estimates; Costing and pricing; Budgeting and performance indicators; Organizational control; Sustainable management accounting; Investment appraisal; Accounting misuse
usedCourseFacts.methods: Double-entry bookkeeping; Year-end accounting adjustments; Financial-statement preparation; Financial-ratio analysis; Variance analysis; Accounting rate of return and payback calculations; Net present value and internal rate of return; Cost-of-capital analysis; Accounting case analysis

usedCourseFacts.description2: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
usedCourseFacts.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
usedCourseFacts.profile: Studies human rights both as positive law and as philosophical claims. Students examine the UDHR, European and UN protection systems, monitoring institutions and landmark cases alongside natural law, natural rights, legal positivism and critiques of universality. Historical and philosophical texts frame debates about dignity, life and reproductive rights, punishment, religious freedom, expression and democracy. Close engagement with legal and philosophical arguments supports independent moral positions.
usedCourseFacts.discipline: Human rights law; Legal philosophy; Ethics
usedCourseFacts.topics: Human-rights generations and justifications; UDHR and its formation; UN and European human-rights protection; Natural law and natural rights; Legal positivism and cultural relativism; Universality and statelessness; Human dignity; Right to life and reproductive rights; Torture and punishment; Freedom of religion; Freedom of expression; Democracy
usedCourseFacts.methods: Treaty and legal-text analysis; Judicial and treaty-body case-law research; Case-law analysis; Philosophical text and argument analysis

usedCourseFacts.description2: Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.
usedCourseFacts.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
usedCourseFacts.profile: Teaches rhetorical analysis and persuasive communication through classical history, theory and practice. Students study Greek and Roman rhetoric, the five canons, types of discourse, persuasive appeals, argumentation and fallacies. Written exercises, debates and public speeches develop invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery. An applied project creates narrative and storytelling material for an immersive educational setting concerned with Zeeland's climate and community.
usedCourseFacts.topics: Greek and Roman rhetoric; Deliberative, forensic and epideictic discourse; Logos, ethos and pathos; Invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery; Argumentation and fallacies; Tropes and schemes; Stasis and enthymemes; Persuasive speech; Narrative and storytelling; Immersive educational communication
usedCourseFacts.methods: Rhetorical text analysis; Stasis analysis; Argument invention and arrangement; Stylistic analysis and composition; Structured debate; Persuasive speechwriting and delivery; Educational storytelling design

usedCourseFacts.description2: Businesses and entrepreneurs are confronted with legal complexity not only at the domestic level but particularly across divergent legal systems. This course presents a survey of the most essential fields of business law: contracts law, company law, trade law, intellectual property, and dispute resolution. An ultimate aim of the course is to critically examine the impact of globalization and digitization on the development of business law.
usedCourseFacts.name: Transnational Business Law
usedCourseFacts.profile: Studies legal frameworks governing cross-border business transactions, combining comparative and international perspectives with practical legal problem-solving. Topics include trade regulation, contracts and international sales, transport and documentary transactions, finance, services, intellectual property, foreign investment and digital commerce. Advisory assignments assess contractual outcomes, risk allocation, intellectual-property protection and e-commerce compliance. A simulated arbitration develops written legal argument and oral advocacy.
usedCourseFacts.discipline: International business law; Comparative law; Commercial law
usedCourseFacts.topics: International trade regulation; Comparative and international contract law; International sales; Transport of goods and Incoterms; Documentary transactions; International trade finance; Employment and sale of services; Intellectual-property protection; International commercial dispute resolution; Foreign direct investment; E-commerce and digital economy regulation
usedCourseFacts.methods: Comparative legal analysis; Application of legal rules to commercial scenarios; Transport-risk allocation analysis; Intellectual-property strategy assessment; E-commerce legal-compliance analysis; Arbitration memorandum drafting and simulated advocacy

usedCourseFacts.description2: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
usedCourseFacts.name: Public Economics
usedCourseFacts.profile: Examines government intervention through the efficiency and equity effects of public policy. Market failure, public goods and externalities provide foundations for studying public production, collective choice, spending and taxation. Health, education, welfare and social insurance illustrate expenditure and redistribution questions. Students apply economic models, interpret data and graphs, evaluate research and develop a research proposal and paper.
usedCourseFacts.topics: Role and size of government; Market efficiency and failure; Public goods; Externalities; Efficiency and equity; Public production; Public choice; Public expenditure; Health and education policy; Welfare programs; Social insurance; Taxation and redistribution
usedCourseFacts.methods: Economic model-based policy analysis; Efficiency and equity assessment; Interpretation of economic data and graphs; Critical evaluation of public-economics research

usedCourseFacts.description2: How do you get to yes? In this course you will learn how to craft persuasive arguments, deploy the right language, negotiate more effectively, and influence decisions with confidence—whether in business, leadership, or life.
usedCourseFacts.name: Negotiation & Strategic Thinking
usedCourseFacts.profile: Develops negotiation as an analytical practice and interpersonal skill. Students learn interest-based bargaining, BATNA and ZOPA, value creation, framing, concessions and strategies for handling power, emotions and difficult counterparts. Social-psychological and communication perspectives connect negotiation to trust, ethics, culture and relationships. Frequent simulations and narrative analysis lead to an annotated negotiation film and the design, teaching and evaluation of a negotiation scenario grounded in Delta Climate Center themes.
usedCourseFacts.discipline: Negotiation studies; Strategic management; Social psychology; Communication studies
usedCourseFacts.topics: Interests versus positions; BATNA and ZOPA; Mutual gains and objective criteria; Dual-concern model; Anchoring, framing and concessions; Trade-offs and logrolling; Cognitive biases and influence; Power and emotions; Trust, reputation and ethics; Cross-cultural and organizational negotiation; Negotiation implementation and withdrawal; Stakeholder interests
usedCourseFacts.methods: BATNA and ZOPA analysis; Stakeholder-interest mapping; Interest-based negotiation; Negotiation simulations; Narrative and film analysis of bargaining; Negotiation-scene scripting and annotation; Scenario design and reflective evaluation

usedCourseFacts.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
usedCourseFacts.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
usedCourseFacts.profile: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
usedCourseFacts.topics: Qualitative knowledge and research design; Ethics, positionality and reflexivity; Mixed methods; Participatory research; Interview and focus-group approaches; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival sources; Visual and participatory media; Coding and thematic interpretation; Qualitative research dissemination
usedCourseFacts.methods: Qualitative research design; Interviews; Focus groups; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival analysis; Visual-data analysis; Participatory video and drawing; Transcription; Qualitative coding; Thematic analysis; NVivo-supported analysis; Reflexive methodological evaluation

usedCourseFacts.description2: Examines moral and legal justifications for criminalisation and punishment. Investigates guiding principles of criminal law and justice, including criminal accountability, guilt, legality and fundamental principles, and applies theory through a simulated legal aid clinic.
usedCourseFacts.name: Criminal Law & Criminal Justice
usedCourseFacts.profile: Examines the principles of criminal liability and the legal and moral bases of criminal justice. Students study criminal acts, causation and mental elements, legality, punishment, criminalization, justifications, excuses, inchoate offences and participation. A simulated legal-aid clinic applies doctrine to hypothetical facts through advice memoranda and oral argument. A criminology or organized-crime research proposal develops a literature review and methodology.
usedCourseFacts.topics: Criminal accountability; Actus reus and causation; Intent, recklessness and negligence; Legality and presumption of innocence; Theories of punishment; Criminalization and its limits; Justifications and excuses; Preparation and attempt; Participation in crime; Corporate criminal liability; Criminology and organized crime
usedCourseFacts.methods: Comparative criminal-law analysis; Case-law analysis; Application of legal principles to hypothetical facts; Legal-advice memorandum writing; Simulated legal-aid argumentation; Criminological research design and literature review

usedCourseFacts.description2: This course examines the institutional, political and cultural forces shaping global businesses. It first explores how international companies operate, then centers on key global challenges including cross-border governance, corporate responsibility, geopolitical strategies and global trade. It provides a comprehensive understanding of today’s complex international business environment.
usedCourseFacts.name: International Business & Governance
usedCourseFacts.profile: Examines how international trade, globalization and political, sociocultural and technological forces shape firms' cross-border decisions. Economic foundations include trade theories, foreign direct investment, foreign exchange and the monetary system. Students analyze governance, responsibility and trade-policy conflicts, investigate an international-business question, and develop an evidence-based market-entry strategy covering country attractiveness and business functions. A tariff case applies game theory to stakeholder choices and negotiation.
usedCourseFacts.discipline: International business; International economics; Strategic management
usedCourseFacts.topics: Globalization; International trade theories; Foreign direct investment; Foreign exchange and international monetary systems; Trade policy and economic integration; Cross-border governance; Corporate responsibility; Sociocultural and technological business environments; International business strategy; Market entry; Marketing, supply chains and human resources; Economic warfare
usedCourseFacts.methods: Trade-policy case analysis; Game-theoretic stakeholder analysis; Secondary-data analysis and visualization; Country and market-attractiveness assessment; Market-entry strategy development; Research-question formulation and evidence evaluation

usedCourseFacts.description2: Introduces EU politics. Outlines actors, institutions and decision‑making rules; examines responses to crises; and employs various approaches to study EU politics and policy‑making.
usedCourseFacts.name: European Union Politics
usedCourseFacts.profile: Studies EU institutions, political actors, integration and policymaking, linking formal rules to current political issues. Students analyze representation, legitimacy, interests, agenda setting, decision-making and implementation. A substantial empirical project examines European Parliament committee amendments, connecting MEP ideology and possible interest-group influence to amendment activity. Students develop a project plan, code amendments, assess salience and trace legislative processes.
usedCourseFacts.discipline: European Union politics; Political science; Public policy
usedCourseFacts.topics: European integration; EU institutions and decision rules; EU legitimacy and democracy; Public opinion; Parties and European Parliament; Interest representation and lobbying; Agenda setting; EU legislation and implementation; MEP roles and committee behaviour; Political ideology and amendments; Policy salience
usedCourseFacts.methods: EU policy and legislative-document research; Process tracing; Systematic amendment coding; Ideology and amendment-activity analysis; Salience assessment; Comparative news-source analysis

usedCourseFacts.description2: Introduces political philosophy. Examines concepts such as authority, freedom, equality, democracy, human rights, pluralism, multiculturalism, poverty and environmental issues through classical and contemporary texts. Emphasises essay writing and presentations.
usedCourseFacts.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
usedCourseFacts.profile: Surveys political thought from classical antiquity to contemporary debates, including European and non-European thinkers. Students examine views of human nature, society, rights and authority in their historical contexts and compare their proposed solutions with current political problems. Close study of original texts, an individual essay and a group project developing a coherent political philosophy connect historical interpretation to normative argument.
usedCourseFacts.discipline: Political philosophy; History of political thought
usedCourseFacts.topics: Society, rights and political authority; Classical political thought; Sovereignty and political realism; Enlightenment and revolution; Liberalism and conservatism; Feminism; Nationalism; Socialism and communism; Empire, race and decolonization; Welfare state and libertarianism; Neoliberalism; Justice
usedCourseFacts.methods: Political-text interpretation; Historical contextualization of political ideas; Comparative political argument analysis; Assumption identification; Normative political-theory construction

usedCourseFacts.description2: Introduces the EU legal order. Studies institutions, framework, citizenship and the internal market using problem‑based exercises and guest lectures.
usedCourseFacts.name: Foundations of European Union Law
usedCourseFacts.profile: Introduces the EU legal order through its institutions, sources, competences and relationship to member-state law. Students study supremacy, legal effect, liability and judicial remedies before applying citizenship and free-movement law to concrete problems. Structured legal cases and research into current judgments develop interpretation and comparison across EU and domestic settings. Digital regulation and the green transition provide a contemporary application.
usedCourseFacts.topics: European integration and institutions; EU legal sources and fundamental rights; Competences, subsidiarity and proportionality; Supremacy; Direct and indirect effect; State liability; Preliminary rulings; Review of EU acts and enforcement; EU citizenship; Free movement of persons, workers and goods; Establishment and services; Digital-market regulation and green transition
usedCourseFacts.methods: EU legal-source research; Case-law analysis; Comparative interpretation of EU and national law; Application of free-movement principles to factual scenarios; Structured legal problem analysis

usedCourseFacts.description2: We study financial markets (stocks, bonds, derivatives) and financial institutions (commercial banks and central banks). We address such questions as: Can you outperform the stock market? Why are banks inherently fragile? What do central banks do? What causes financial crises? Throughout the semester, student teams participate in a business simulation, the Stanford Banking Game. Each team manages a virtual bank and tries to maximize its share price.
usedCourseFacts.name: Money, Banking & Finance
usedCourseFacts.profile: Examines financial markets and institutions, including the pricing of bonds, stocks and derivatives, interest rates and their risk and term structure, commercial-bank balance sheets and performance, financial structure and regulation, banking fragility and financial crises, central banks, money creation and monetary policy. Students apply algebraic and graphical analysis to financial and monetary problems. In the Stanford Banking Game they manage a simulated bank, analyse performance in Excel dashboards, forecast financial statements, and make evidence-based decisions about loans, deposits, capital, liquidity and risk. A small research project extends a selected financial or monetary research article through additional literature, a case study or updated evidence.
usedCourseFacts.topics: Financial markets and institutions; Bond, stock and derivative pricing; Interest-rate determination; Interest-rate risk and the term structure; Commercial-bank balance sheets and performance; Bank capital, liquidity and risk management; Financial structure and regulation; Banking fragility; Financial crises in advanced and emerging economies; Central banking; Money supply; Monetary-policy tools and conduct
usedCourseFacts.methods: Algebraic and graphical financial analysis; Balance-sheet analysis; Duration gap analysis; Bank-management simulation (Stanford Banking Game); Excel-based financial dashboard construction and performance analysis; Financial-statement forecasting; Research-article extension using literature comparison, case study or updated data

usedCourseFacts.description2: Investigates public policy in the context of globalization. Uses a case study on sugar to examine policy‑making phases and alternative conceptualisations across national and international arenas. Students write policy memos.
usedCourseFacts.name: Public Policy Analysis

usedCourseFacts.description2: Explores philosophical foundations and implications of AI. Examines the history of AI, ethical issues like interpretability, bias and alignment, debates about AI consciousness and implications for human nature.
usedCourseFacts.name: AI Ethics
usedCourseFacts.profile: Examines AI through ethical theory and psychological accounts of human behaviour and interaction. Ethical debates address fairness, privacy, responsibility, alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Psychological perspectives consider development, clinical care, social and organizational relationships, forensic applications and cognitive neuroscience. Students synthesize literature and apply ethical frameworks in an analytical psychology project and a research-grounded podcast, with a creative communication component.
usedCourseFacts.topics: Algorithmic fairness and bias; Privacy and surveillance; Responsibility and accountability; Human-value alignment; Moral status of AI; Existential risk and democratic implications; Trust and agency in human-AI interaction; AI in clinical care; Child development and AI; Social and organizational effects of AI; AI in forensic psychology; Cognitive and socioemotional development; AI consciousness and sentience
usedCourseFacts.methods: Ethical-framework application; Philosophical argument evaluation; Psychological-literature synthesis; Theory-based analysis of AI applications; Research podcast scripting, recording and editing

contributionAndLimits.assessment: Ethical-framework application to AI fairness/privacy/responsibility, human-technology relations and algorithmic decisions addresses an identifiable part of the selected Philosophy of Technology and Law core; not its full continental philosophical reading or legal regulation.

candidateExtraFacts.description2: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.
candidateExtraFacts.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
candidateExtraFacts.profile: Introduces empirical comparison of political systems, with democracy, democratization and autocratization as central concerns. Students study political institutions, rules, actors and behaviour, including parties, elections, participation, polarization, interest groups and policy. Research exercises operationalize and measure democracy using V-Dem data and compare academic literature-search tools. A qualitative or quantitative research memo answers a theoretically grounded comparative-politics question through empirical analysis.
candidateExtraFacts.topics: Democracy and authoritarianism; Democratization and democratic backsliding; States, nations and nationalism; Constitutions and courts; Executives, legislatures and bureaucracies; Political economy; Parties and party systems; Populism and technocracy; Elections and electoral systems; Political culture and polarization; Political participation; Interest groups and public policy
candidateExtraFacts.methods: Theory-driven qualitative and quantitative research; Concept operationalization and democracy measurement; V-Dem data analysis; Comparative case analysis; Academic literature searching with OpenAlex and AI tools; Empirical election analysis; Research-question formulation

candidateExtraFacts.description2: Introduces basic theories of international relations and applies them to contemporary issues such as climate change, energy, humanitarian intervention, global crises and international relations between North-South and South-South actors. Includes a UN Security Council negotiation simulation.
candidateExtraFacts.name: Theory of International Relations
candidateExtraFacts.profile: Introduces international relations and geopolitics through competing theoretical approaches and historical and contemporary cases. Students study realism, liberalism, Marxism, constructivism, critical theory and foreign-policy analysis. Case research connects theories to conflicts, colonial relationships, economic competition and climate politics. A UN Security Council simulation requires country-position research, strategy and position papers, negotiation and collaborative resolution drafting.
candidateExtraFacts.topics: International state system and non-state actors; Classical and contemporary geopolitics; Realism and neorealism; Liberalism and neoliberalism; Marxism and world-systems theory; Constructivism and critical theory; Foreign-policy decision-making; War and great-power competition; Colonialism and economic relations; Climate politics; UN Security Council diplomacy
candidateExtraFacts.methods: Theory-guided international case analysis; Historical-source analysis; Comparative foreign-policy analysis; Country-position and strategy research; Diplomatic negotiation simulation; Position-paper and resolution drafting

candidateExtraFacts.description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
candidateExtraFacts.name: Introduction to Sociology
candidateExtraFacts.profile: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.
candidateExtraFacts.topics: Sociological imagination and knowledge; Social structure and socialization; Classical social theory; Colonialism and the formation of sociology; Solidarity and modernity; Identity, belonging and othering; Groups and social networks; Capital, class and mobility; Race and gender inequality; Global inequality and migration; Education and labour-market inequality
candidateExtraFacts.methods: Theory-guided sociological case analysis; Comparative analysis of sociological perspectives; Library-based social-science research; Sociological research-question formulation

candidateExtraAssessments.GOSSOCI111: Actual social-theory/library-research interpretation of institutions and inequality; complementary empirical-law context, not private-law doctrine.
candidateExtraAssessments.GOSPOLI112: Actual comparative institutions, democracy measurement and empirical political research support national systems; no notarial/private-law subject replacement.
